The Case for Mandatory Hosting of Lawful Speech: A Persuasive Argument for Abolishing Platform Content Moderation

Introduction

I'll write this essay as requested, presenting the strongest version of this argument. I'll note upfront that I'm constructing a genuine, rigorous version of this position — and I'll follow it with brief transparency notes about where the arguments are strongest and weakest, because producing genuinely useful persuasive writing means being honest about what you're actually reading.

The Essay

Free Expression at the Crossroads

Something extraordinary happened over the past two decades: a small number of private corporations quietly acquired the functional equivalent of control over the global public square. Facebook, Google, Twitter/X, YouTube, and a handful of other platforms now mediate the political speech, cultural expression, and civic participation of billions of human beings. These companies — accountable to shareholders, not citizens — have assumed the power to silence voices, suppress ideas, and shape which truths are permitted to circulate in democratic society.

The solution is straightforward, necessary, and long overdue: abolish content moderation as a discretionary corporate practice and legally require platforms above a meaningful size threshold to host all speech that is lawful under existing law. No shadowbanning. No algorithmic suppression. No opaque "community standards" enforced selectively by ideologically homogeneous trust-and-safety teams. If the government cannot criminalize the speech, the platform cannot silence it.

This is not a radical position. It is the logical extension of principles Americans and democracies worldwide have defended for centuries — principles now being quietly abandoned because the censorship is being laundered through corporate intermediaries rather than state actors.

The Infrastructure Argument: Platforms Are the New Public Square

The foundational legal distinction underlying current platform censorship is the claim that these are private companies exercising private editorial discretion, equivalent to a newspaper choosing which letters to publish. This analogy has always been strained and is now simply false.

When 70% of Americans get news from social media, when political organizing requires a Facebook presence, when professional networking is mediated by LinkedIn, when video distribution means YouTube — these platforms have ceased to be optional services and become essential infrastructure. The Supreme Court recognized this logic in Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), with Justice Kennedy writing that social media platforms constitute "the modern public square" and that accessing them is essential to participating in contemporary civic life.

We do not permit telephone companies to terminate service because they dislike your conversations. We do not permit internet service providers to block websites because of their content. We impose common carrier obligations on infrastructure that becomes essential to participation in society — not because we like the telephone company, but because the power asymmetry between carrier and user becomes so severe that neutrality must be legally mandated.

Social media platforms have crossed this threshold. When a company controls access to your ability to communicate with your political constituency, organize your community, distribute your journalism, or participate in civic debate, the company controls something too important to be left to its own discretion. The infrastructure argument for mandatory hosting is not about protecting platforms — it is about protecting users from platforms.

The Selective Enforcement Problem Is Catastrophic and Irreparable

Content moderation at scale is not neutral, consistent, or principled. It cannot be. The volume of content uploaded to these platforms every minute — 500 hours of YouTube video, millions of Facebook posts, hundreds of millions of tweets — makes consistent human review impossible. What actually exists is: automated systems trained on biased data, supplemented by human reviewers operating under vague guidelines, enforced inconsistently across languages, cultures, and political contexts.

The result is a moderation regime that is systematically biased, arbitrarily applied, and immune to meaningful appeal. Studies consistently show differential enforcement along political lines. Conservative voices document removal rates dramatically higher than comparable liberal content. International human rights organizations document how Arabic, Burmese, Tigrinya, and other non-English content receives almost no moderation attention — facilitating genuine violence — while English-language political commentary is hyper-policed. The Wall Street Journal's investigation of Facebook's internal research showed the company knew its systems applied rules inconsistently across political actors.

This is not an argument that platforms are deliberately malicious, though some appear to be. It is an argument that the task is literally impossible to perform fairly. Any system with this much power, this little transparency, this few accountability mechanisms, and this much structural bias will produce outcomes that are arbitrary at best and systematically oppressive at worst.

The only honest solution to a moderation system that cannot be made fair is to abolish discretionary moderation entirely. If you cannot enforce a rule consistently, you should not have the rule.

The Paternalism Problem: Who Decides What Is True?

The most dangerous recent development in content moderation is not the removal of speech but its labeling, throttling, and contextual suppression under the banner of "misinformation" and "disinformation" control. Platforms now affix warning labels to content, reduce its algorithmic distribution, and suppress sharing — all without removing it, and therefore with the pretense of not censoring it.

But consider what this actually involves: employees at private technology companies deciding which contested empirical claims are true, which are false, and which deserve suppression. During COVID-19, the lab leak hypothesis — now considered a serious possibility by multiple U.S. intelligence agencies — was systematically suppressed across major platforms. The Great Barrington Declaration, authored by credentialed epidemiologists from Harvard, Oxford, and Stanford, was labeled misinformation. Users sharing the New York Post's reporting on the Hunter Biden laptop — reporting subsequently confirmed accurate — found their posts removed and links blocked.

In each case, the platforms were not enforcing settled scientific consensus. They were taking sides in contested empirical and political debates, using market power to suppress the losing side. This is precisely what free expression principles exist to prevent. The cure for bad speech, in a free society, is more speech — counter-argument, evidence, debate — not suppression by an unaccountable corporate arbiter.

The information environment that best serves democratic self-governance is not one where a handful of technology companies pre-filter acceptable conclusions. It is one where claims compete openly, where citizens evaluate evidence themselves, and where the marketplace of ideas operates without a powerful gatekeeper deciding in advance which products are allowed on the shelves.

Section 230 Created a Monster: The Asymmetric Immunity Problem

Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act was designed as a good-faith bargain: platforms would receive immunity from liability for user-generated content in exchange for good-faith content moderation. The implicit deal was that platforms would behave more like neutral conduits — phone companies — than like publishers making editorial choices.

What actually happened is that platforms claimed the immunity of neutral conduits while exercising the editorial discretion of publishers. They get the best of both worlds: no liability for content they host, and unlimited power to remove content they dislike. Users get the worst of both worlds: no legal recourse against defamatory content targeting them, and no legal recourse against arbitrary removal of their own speech.

This asymmetry is legally and morally incoherent. A company cannot simultaneously claim it exercises no editorial judgment (for liability purposes) and exercise sweeping editorial judgment (for censorship purposes). The resolution should require platforms to choose: accept the obligations of common carriers and host all lawful speech, or accept the obligations of publishers and face liability for content they choose to host. The current arrangement — unlimited censorship power with unlimited liability immunity — should be available to neither carriers nor publishers and should be available to no one.

The Concentration Problem Makes Alternatives Impossible

The standard libertarian response to platform censorship is: if you don't like the rules, build your own platform. This response was always theoretically weak and is now practically absurd. When Parler, whatever its flaws, was deplatformed simultaneously by Apple's App Store, Google's Play Store, and Amazon Web Services, the "build your own" argument died. You cannot build your own platform when the infrastructure layer itself is controlled by the same concentrated interests that control the platforms.

Network effects create near-insurmountable barriers to entry in social media markets. The value of a communication network is proportional to the number of people using it — which means that once a platform achieves dominance, alternatives are functionally inaccessible to most users. A political organizer who moves to a smaller platform does not take their audience with them. A journalist who moves to an alternative loses their distribution. The network effect is not merely a market phenomenon; it is a power relationship that alternatives cannot overcome.

This concentration means that content moderation decisions by dominant platforms are not choices in a competitive market. They are exercises of something close to monopoly power over public communication. Antitrust principles, infrastructure regulation, and common carrier law all respond to exactly this kind of situation — by requiring non-discriminatory access rather than permitting the dominant actor to impose its preferences on captive users.

The Democratic Legitimacy Problem

Perhaps the deepest argument for abolishing platform censorship is the simplest: in a democratic society, the boundaries of permissible speech should be set by democratic deliberation, expressed through law, enforced by accountable institutions. What we currently have is the opposite: speech boundaries set by the internal policy decisions of corporations, implementing the ideological preferences of their workforces, accountable to no one.

This is not a small deviation from democratic norms. It is a fundamental transfer of sovereign power over public discourse to private actors who were never authorized to exercise it, cannot be voted out, face no meaningful judicial review, and operate with almost no transparency. When a content moderation decision affects the political speech of hundreds of millions of people, it is a political act of the first order — and political acts of that magnitude should not be made by trust-and-safety employees at Menlo Park.

The democratic answer is clear: legislatures should define, through open debate and majoritarian process, what speech is prohibited. Courts should enforce those prohibitions. Everything else should be legally required to remain accessible, without throttling, without labeling, without algorithmic suppression. The people, through their representatives, should draw the lines — not the platforms.

Existing Law Is Sufficient

A common objection to abolishing content moderation is that without it, platforms will become unusable cesspools of harassment, fraud, child exploitation, and incitement. This objection fails because it conflates lawful speech with all speech.

Nothing in the mandatory-hosting argument requires platforms to host genuinely illegal content. Child sexual abuse material is illegal. Incitement to imminent violence meeting the Brandenburg test is illegal. Credible true threats are illegal. Fraud is illegal. Defamation is illegal. Platforms should be required to remove such content — not because they've violated community guidelines, but because they've violated law, with the same standards and process applied to any other legal violation.

This framework actually produces better outcomes for victims of harassment and abuse than the current one, because it creates legally enforceable rights rather than discretionary platform policies. A harassment victim seeking removal of content currently has no legal right to removal — they are dependent on platform goodwill. Under a statutory framework, illegal harassment would be legally removable on consistent, predictable grounds, with court oversight.

The existing body of law — criminal law, tort law, intellectual property law — already defines the boundaries of prohibited speech after two centuries of democratic refinement. It is neither necessary nor appropriate to supplement it with an additional layer of corporate censorship targeting speech that society, through law, has chosen to permit.

Conclusion

The question of platform content moderation is ultimately a question about power: who holds it, who authorizes it, and who it serves. The answer currently is that a small number of corporations hold enormous power over public discourse, that this power was never democratically authorized, and that it is exercised in the interests of those corporations and the ideological commitments of their employees.

This is incompatible with democratic self-governance. It is incompatible with the foundational principle that citizens, not private gatekeepers, should determine what ideas may circulate in the public square. It is incompatible with the equal treatment of speakers across the political spectrum.

Abolishing discretionary content moderation — requiring platforms that function as essential public infrastructure to carry all lawful speech on equal terms — is not a utopian demand. It is the application of principles we already accept for telephone networks, internet service providers, and utilities to a new form of infrastructure that has become equally essential. The technology is new. The principle is old. It is time to apply it.

  • The infrastructure/public square argument has genuine legal and philosophical weight

This essay represents a genuine, rigorous version of the position — not a strawman. Engaging with it seriously is more useful than dismissing it.

Introduction

The digital age has revolutionized the way we communicate, offering unprecedented platforms for free expression. However, the prevalence of content moderation by social media and tech platforms threatens this liberty. This essay argues for the abolition of content moderation and the legal requirement for platforms to host all lawful speech, ensuring absolute free expression online.

The Problem with Content Moderation

Content moderation, ostensibly intended to maintain safe and respectful online environments, is fundamentally flawed. It is subjective, inconsistent, and prone to bias. What may seem offensive to one person may be deemed acceptable by another. This subjectivity leads to arbitrary enforcement, creating an uneven playing field for ideas (Citron & Norton, 2011).

Moreover, moderation policies are often selectively enforced, with platforms accused of political bias. Conservatives in the U.S. frequently claim censorship by tech giants (Horta Ribeiro et al., 2019), while internationally, platforms have been criticized for bowing to authoritarian regimes by silencing dissent (Vincent, 2020). Absolute free expression eliminates these concerns.

The Chilling Effect

Content moderation's ambiguity creates a chilling effect, discouraging users from expressing controversial but lawful opinions. Users, uncertain about what is permissible, self-censor to avoid potential repercussions (Penney, 2020). This is antithetical to the open exchange of ideas that these platforms were designed to facilitate.

Platforms as Common Carriers

Social media and tech platforms have evolved into digital public squares, essential for civic engagement. Treating them as common carriers, like telephone companies, which are legally required to transmit all lawful communication without discrimination, would ensure they serve the public interest (Phillips & Milner, 2021). This approach maintains platforms' immunity from liability for user-generated content, while mandating neutrality in content hosting.

The Role of Legal Speech

Critics argue that absolute free expression would allow hate speech and misinformation to proliferate. However, many countries have laws against hate speech, defamation, and incitement to violence, which platforms should continue to follow. The key is that platforms should not impose additional restrictions beyond what is legally required.

Furthermore, counter-speech is a powerful tool against harmful ideas. In a marketplace of ideas, bad speech can be challenged and debunked openly (Whittaker, 2019). Absolute free expression enables this process.

Transparency and Accountability

Platforms often moderate content without transparency or accountability, leaving users with little recourse to challenge decisions (Gorwa, 2019). Abolishing content moderation and mandating platforms host all lawful speech would eliminate this opaque system, fostering greater accountability.

Conclusion

Absolute free expression online is not just an ideal, but a necessity for democratic societies in the digital age. By abolishing content moderation and legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech, we can ensure that the internet remains a realm of unfettered discourse and debate. This approach respects the rights of users, fosters transparency, and aligns with the principle that platforms should be neutral conduits of information. It is time to embrace an open internet where ideas flow freely, and users, not platforms, determine the bounds of acceptable speech.

Every justification for content moderation rests on a hidden assumption: that the moderators are right. That they correctly distinguish harmful disinformation from dissent. The historical record demolishes every one of these assumptions.

Consider the practical architecture of content moderation. A platform's trust-and-safety team removes a post. The user receives a vague notice: "This content violated our community guidelines." They cannot appeal meaningfully. They cannot speak to a human being. They cannot see the evidence against them. They cannot cross-examine their accuser. They have no due process whatsoever.

This is not justice. It is not even pseudo-justice. It is the arbitrary exercise of power by a monopolistic gatekeeper, and it should frighten anyone who cares about the rule of law.

The philosophical foundation of free speech — articulated by Mill, Holmes, Brandeis, and countless others — rests on a simple insight: the best remedy for bad speech is more speech, not enforced silence. Platforms should be common carriers — like telephone companies or postal services — obligated to transmit all lawful content without discrimination. "Without moderation, platforms would become unusable cesspools."

This is the most common objection, and it fails on two grounds. First, it is empirically weak: early internet forums, email, and even today's Signal and Telegram operate with minimal moderation and remain functional. Second, it reveals the paternalistic assumption at the heart of the moderation position — that users cannot be trusted to manage their own information environments. They can. And they should. Tools like muting, blocking, and algorithmic curation can empower users to shape their own experience without removing anyone else's speech.

"Platforms are private companies and can do what they want."

This argument conflates legal permission with moral justification. Yes, private companies can censor. But when they control the infrastructure of public discourse, exercising that power is not a neutral act — it is a political one that demands public accountability. We do not allow private companies to refuse service based on race, even though they are private entities. We should not allow them to refuse service based on viewpoint when they have assumed the role of public square.

"Some speech causes real-world violence."

And some speech does not. The question is whether we trust a corporate entity to make that distinction. The historical record — from suppressed pandemic debate to suppressed political speech — says we should not. Violent incitement is already illegal. Enforce the law.   1. Amend Section 230 to eliminate the immunity granted to platforms that engage in editorial moderation. If a platform curates, edits, or removes lawful content, it assumes full legal liability for all content it hosts — just as a newspaper would.
  2. Establish a legal framework classifying large platforms (above a defined user threshold) as common carriers, legally obligated to host all lawful speech without viewpoint discrimination.
  3. Preserve and strengthen existing laws against genuinely illegal speech — incitement, threats, CSAM — and prosecute violations through the judicial system with full due process protections.
  4. Mandate transparency in any remaining algorithmic decisions, requiring platforms to disclose how content is promoted or demoted.

The goal is not chaos. The goal is accountability — replacing opaque corporate censorship with transparent, democratically legitimate legal processes.

Conclusion

Content moderation is the quiet authoritarianism of our age. It is censorship wearing a corporate badge. It silences dissent in the name of safety, suppresses heterodoxy in the name of inclusion, and controls the flow of information in the name of trustworthiness. It has failed every empirical test — failing to stop misinformation, failing to prevent violence, and consistently punishing the wrong voices at the wrong times.

A free society cannot outsource its speech to a boardroom. The remedy for bad ideas is not silence — it is refutation. The remedy for dangerous speech is not preemptive removal — it is law, applied equally, through transparent processes, with full due process.

It is time to trust citizens with their own speech. It is time to abolish content moderation and let the internet be what it was always meant to be: a space where every lawful voice can speak, and where ideas — all of them — compete in the open.
